items.description: Average household water use per person per day, by use, for a New Zealand household on its own supply
items.note: ESR Table 1. Drinking here is the 2 L the table allows; the island books what each body actually turns over (1 mL/kcal) instead, so it uses the other rows for the household.

items.description: Water to store per person per day after an emergency: enough for drinking, cooking, washing hands, dishes and a sponge bath, but not a shower or laundry; and the bare minimum for drinking and cooking alone
items.note: ESR p. 29, citing BRANZ (2008). The island uses 'rationed' as what a household cuts back to when its tank runs low.

items.description: Rain lost per day before a roof delivers water to its tank (first-flush diverter, leaking spouting, inefficient collection): inflow = (daily rainfall - loss) x roof area
items.note: Section 2.1, equation 1; the 1 mm was agreed with Greater Wellington as a modelling assumption, and the whole roof area is taken as effective.

items.description: Capacity of the largest common rainwater tank: conventional above-ground cylindrical tanks 'generally have the highest volume, with single tanks holding up to 30,000 litres'
items.note: The island installs whole tanks of this size, as many as the estate's driest run needs and never fewer than one.

items.description: Typical on-site storage for a household solely dependent on rainwater tanks
items.note: A community flyer, used only as a cross-check on the installed size, never as an input. The same flyer recommends 30,000-50,000 L for homes of three or more bedrooms.

items.description: A rigid plastic water jerrycan of the size recommended for family use: its capacity and its empty weight
items.note: What a founder fetches water in when the tank is dry.
